تُعدّ المسرحية من أعمق الدراسات الأدبية في الطموح المدمّر والضمير المعذَّب. شخصية ماكبث نموذج إنساني فريد: بطل يعرف أن فعله شرير ويفعله مع ذلك، ثم يعيش في جحيم داخلي. والمسرحية من أقصر أعمال شكسبير وأكثرها كثافة شعرية، ومن أجمل ما فيها مونولوج الخنجر ومشهد السير في النوم الشهير.
context: كتبها شكسبير في عهد الملك جيمس الأول الذي كان مفتوناً بالسحر والتنجيم، ويُرجَّح أن المسرحية أُلّفت لتُعجبه. تقع أحداثها في اسكتلندا القرن الحادي عشر، وتستند إلى وقائع تاريخية حقيقية وإن حرّفها شكسبير لأغراضه الدرامية. والمسرحية تعيش على المسارح حتى اليوم وقد أُخرجت عشرات المرات سينمائياً، من أبرزها فيلم أكيرا كوروساوا «عرش الدم» 1957 المأخوذ عن روحها.

about: Macbeth is one of Shakespeare's most intense tragedies, written around 1606. A Scottish general, spurred by a prophecy and his wife's ambition, murders King Duncan to seize the throne — only to descend into paranoia and tyranny. The play is a powerful study of unchecked ambition and guilt.
context: Written for King James I, who was fascinated by witchcraft. The play draws on real Scottish history but reshapes it for dramatic effect. One of Shakespeare's shortest plays, it remains a staple of world theatre and has inspired countless film adaptations.

about: «دفاع سقراط» نص أفلاطون الذي يروي فيه خطاب سقراط أمام محكمة أثينا عام 399 قبل الميلاد، حين حوكم بتهمة إفساد الشباب وإهانة الآلهة. سقراط لا يدافع عن نفسه بمعنى الكلمة بل يشرح رسالته الفلسفية بلا خوف.

هذا الخطاب هو أول وثيقة في تاريخ الفلسفة الغربية عن حق الفرد في اتباع ضميره أمام الدولة. جملته «الحياة غير المفحوصة لا تستحق أن تُعاش» من أشهر ما قاله الفلاسفة في التاريخ كله. نُدان سقراط ومات بشرب السم وهو يسلّم.
context: أفلاطون كان حاضراً في المحاكمة. هذا النص مع «الكريتو» و«فيدو» يُشكّل ثلاثية موت سقراط. مقرر في معظم مناهج الفلسفة الجامعية في العالم.

about: Plato's Apology records Socrates' speech at his trial in Athens (399 BCE), where he was condemned to death for corrupting youth and impiety. Rather than defending himself, Socrates defends the life of philosophical inquiry. 'The unexamined life is not worth living' — one of philosophy's most quoted lines.
context: Plato was present at the trial. Forms a trilogy with Crito and Phaedo covering Socrates' final days. Required reading in nearly every university philosophy course worldwide.

about: «مغامرات شيرلوك هولمز» المجموعة الأولى لقصص كونان دويل عن أشهر محقق في التاريخ، نُشرت عام 1892. اثنتا عشرة قصة تعرض الأسلوب الاستنتاجي الفريد لهولمز وصاحبه الدكتور واتسون في شوارع لندن الفيكتورية.

هولمز هو المحقق الخيالي الأوحد الذي دفع الناس إلى البحث عن عنوانه الحقيقي. الجمع بين الطابع الغريب للقضايا والمنطق الصارم والزمان الفيكتوري ولغة دويل المتيسرة جعل هذه القصص مؤسسة للأدب البوليسي كله. «عصبة ذوي الشعر الأحمر» و«وقفة الرجل المتعلم» من أحسن ما في الأدب القصصي القصير.
context: أراد دويل قتل هولمز مرة واحدة والتفرغ للتاريخ، لكن ضغط القراء أعاده. كتابته المسلسلة في مجلة ستراند جعلتها من أكثر قصص التاريخ مبيعاً.

about: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (1892) collects twelve stories featuring the detective's razor-sharp deductive method and Dr Watson's loyal narration. Holmes and Victorian London are inseparable. 'The Red-Headed League' and 'A Scandal in Bohemia' are masterpieces of the short story form.
context: Conan Doyle tried to kill Holmes to write serious history; public outcry forced his return. Holmes' 221B Baker Street address still receives real mail. The template for virtually every detective story that followed.

about: الملحمة اليونانية المنسوبة إلى هوميروس، ثانية ملحمتيه بعد [الإلياذة](/book/172). بعد سقوط طروادة يحاول البطل أوديسيوس العودة إلى بيته في جزيرة إيثاكا، فتستغرق رحلته عشر سنوات يلقى فيها العملاق ذا العين الواحدة، وحوريات البحر الساحرات، والساحرة كيركي، بينما تنتظره زوجته بينيلوبي ويحاصرها الخُطّاب.
context: «الأوديسة» من أقدم آثار الأدب الأوروبي، ونموذج كل قصص الرحلة والعودة التي جاءت بعدها، حتى صار اسمها في لغات كثيرة يعني الرحلة الطويلة الشاقة. نقلها إلى العربية نثراً دريني خشبة وغيره، والنص هنا بترجمة إنجليزية.
وإن لم تقرأ الملاحم من قبل، فابدأ بـ«الأوديسة» لا بـ«الإلياذة»، فمغامراتها أقرب إلى الحكايات، وفصولها تُقرأ كحلقات متتابعة من مسلسل طويل. فاستمتع برحلتها الطويلة.

about: The second of the two epics attributed to Homer, after the [Iliad](/book/172?lang=en). After the fall of Troy, Odysseus spends ten years trying to sail home to Ithaca, meeting the one-eyed Cyclops, the Sirens and the enchantress Circe, while at home his wife Penelope holds off a crowd of suitors.
context: One of the founding works of European literature, it is the model for every story of a long journey home, and its title has become a common word for one. The text here is an English translation.

about: «البعث» آخر روايات تولستوي الكبرى، نُشرت عام 1899، كُتبت لجمع المال لدعم طائفة الدوخوبور المضطهدة. تحكي قصة الأمير نخليودوف الذي يتعرف في قاعة المحاكم على كاتيوشا، فتاةً أغواها في شبابه ثم تركها فأصبحت بائسة وتُحاكَم ظلماً. يقرر إنقاذها ففي ذلك بعثه الروحي.
الرواية نقد شرس للكنيسة الروسية الأرثوذكسية والدولة القيصرية مما أفضى إلى حرمان تولستوي من الكنيسة. الرواية أقل الروايات الثلاث فنياً لكنها الأكثر التزاماً أخلاقياً وصراحةً سياسية.
context: أفضى نشرها إلى حرمان تولستوي كنسياً رسمياً عام 1901. أعاد تولستوي التبرع بكل أرباحها للدوخوبور.

about: Resurrection (1899) follows Prince Nekhlyudov who recognizes in a defendant a woman he seduced and abandoned years ago. His attempts to save her become his own spiritual redemption. Tolstoy's most politically direct novel, and the one that led to his excommunication.
context: Written to fund the persecuted Doukhobor sect. The novel's attacks on the Orthodox Church led to Tolstoy's formal excommunication in 1901.

about: «إشارة الأربعة» الرواية الثانية في سلسلة هولمز، نُشرت عام 1890. مِيري ميوريي تطلب من هولمز التحقيق في رسائل غامضة تتلقاها من شخص مجهول، فيتشعب التحقيق إلى مخطط قتل وكنز مخبأ يمتد تاريخه إلى الهند الاستعمارية.
الرواية تجمع بين الغموض والإثارة وعناصر من رواية المغامرة. مشهد الملاحقة بالزوارق في نهر التيمز من أكثر مشاهد هولمز إثارةً. الرواية كُتبت في ليلة واحدة وفق دويل إثر رهان مع ناشر.
context: كُتبت إثر طلب ناشر أمريكي لرواية ثانية بعد «دراسة في اللون القرمزي». قيل إن دويل كتبها في عشية واحدة. تحتوي على أحد أولى ظهور الكوكايين في الأدب.

about: The Sign of the Four (1890) sends Holmes and Watson after a mystery rooted in colonial India, involving a stolen treasure and a trail of murder. The Thames boat chase is one of the series' most gripping set-pieces. Watson falls in love, giving this novel a warmer tone than most Holmes adventures.
context: Written at the request of an American publisher after 'A Study in Scarlet'. Contains some of the earliest literary depictions of cocaine use — Holmes injects it freely. Established the template for Holmes' longer cases.

about: «أعمال إدغار ألان بو» تضم المجموعة الثانية من قصصه وشعره، وبو من أهم الأصوات في الأدب الأمريكي في القرن التاسع عشر. قصائده «الغراب» و«أنابيل لي» من أجمل ما كُتب شعراً إنجليزياً، وقصصه في الرعب والغموض أسّست لهذين النوعين في الأدب العالمي.
بو لم يُقدَّر في حياته تقديراً كافياً، لكن اعترفت به فرنسا أولاً: بودلير ترجمه وعدّه من أعظم الشعراء. تقنيات الكشف في قصص دوبان أسّست لنوع القصة البوليسية أكثر مما يُعترف له.
context: مات في ظروف غامضة عام 1849 وعمره أربعون. أثّر في بودلير وفالاريه ومالارميه وبرام ستوكر وكونان دويل.

about: Edgar Allan Poe's collected works include Gothic horror, philosophical tales and some of the most musical poetry in English. 'The Raven' and 'Annabel Lee' are among the most quoted English poems. His detective Auguste Dupin stories, often overlooked, invented the detective fiction genre before Conan Doyle.
context: Poe died in mysterious circumstances at forty. Undervalued in America in his lifetime; Baudelaire translated him and championed him in France, securing his European reputation. His influence on Stoker, Conan Doyle and the horror genre is immeasurable.

about: «المقامر» رواية دوستويفسكي القصيرة، نُشرت عام 1866، كتبها في عشرين يوماً بعد اتفاق مع ناشره أو خسر حقوق أعماله. بطلها مدرس روسي يعمل في منتجع أوروبي، يدمنه الروليت ويتعلق بالثرية البارعة بولينا. الرواية نفسها صورة الإدمان الأعمق وأصدقها في الأدب.

دوستويفسكي كتبها من تجربته الشخصية المباشرة كمدمن قمار، ومليئة بالتحليل النفسي للإدمان: اللذة اللحظية وخسارة السيطرة والتدمير الذاتي. تزوج دوستويفسكي بعد انتهاء الرواية من ستينوغرافته التي ساعدته في إتمامها.
context: كتبها بإملاء على ستينوغرافته آنا غريغوريفنا التي صارت زوجته لاحقاً. من أكثر الروايات القصيرة نفسيةً في تصوير الإدمان.

about: The Gambler (1866) was written in twenty days to meet a publisher's deadline. A Russian tutor at a European resort becomes addicted to roulette and obsessed with the beautiful Polina. Drawn from Dostoevsky's own gambling addiction, it is literature's most psychologically acute portrait of compulsive gambling.
context: Dictated to his stenographer Anna, who later became his wife. Written under extreme pressure but captures the psychology of addiction with devastating precision.

about: «الإلياذة» ملحمة هوميروس الكبرى، من أقدم الآداب الغربية وأعظمها، تعود إلى القرن الثامن قبل الميلاد. تحكي الأسابيع الأخيرة من حرب طروادة العاشرة، وتتمحور حول غضب أخيل حين ينتزع منه أغاممنون الجارية بريزيس. لكنها ليست قصة نصر بل قصة إنسانية عن الغضب والشرف والخسارة والموت.

الملحمة تتناوب بين المحاربين اليونانيين والطرواديين بعطف متساوٍ، وهكتور بطل طروادة من أنبل شخصيات الأدب. أبياتها في وصف المعارك تجمع القسوة والجمال معاً. شكّلت الأدب الغربي لثلاثة آلاف سنة وتُقرأ في جامعات العالم كله حتى اليوم.
context: نُقلت شفهياً لقرون قبل تدوينها. مَثّلت مع الأوديسة أساس التعليم الكلاسيكي اليوناني والروماني. ترجمها إلى العربية عدد من الأدباء منهم سليمان البستاني.

about: The Iliad, attributed to Homer (c.8th century BCE), covers the final weeks of the Trojan War through the lens of Achilles' wrath. It balances Greek and Trojan heroes with equal humanity. Hector's farewell to his family is among literature's most moving scenes. The foundation of Western literary tradition.
context: Transmitted orally for centuries before being written down. Formed the core of Greek and Roman education. Alexander the Great slept with a copy under his pillow. Still taught in universities worldwide.

about: رواية دوستويفسكي الشهيرة الصادرة عام 1866. راسكولنيكوف طالب فقير في سانت بطرسبرغ يقنع نفسه بأن الإنسان الاستثنائي يحق له أن يتجاوز القانون، فيقتل مرابية عجوزاً. لا تسأل الرواية «من القاتل؟»، بل «ماذا يفعل القتل بالقاتل؟»: الحمّى والخوف والكذب، ثم مطاردة المحقق الذكي بورفيري، وحب سونيا التي تدلّه على طريق الاعتراف.
context: تُعد «الجريمة والعقاب» من أهم روايات القرن التاسع عشر، لأنها حوّلت رواية الجريمة إلى رحلة داخل الضمير، وناقشت أفكاراً فلسفية عن الأخلاق والحرية والخلاص في قالب مشوّق. تُرجمت إلى العربية مرات كثيرة، أشهرها ترجمة سامي الدروبي ضمن أعمال دوستويفسكي الكاملة.
وإن كانت الرواية طويلة عليك، فاقرأ فصولها الأولى بتمهل، فهي تضعك في عقل راسكولنيكوف المحموم، وبعدها تجرّك الأحداث حتى النهاية.

about: Dostoevsky's 1866 novel follows Raskolnikov, a penniless student in St Petersburg who convinces himself that an extraordinary man may step over the law, and murders an old pawnbroker. The question is not who did it but what the crime does to him: fever, fear and lies, the patient investigator Porfiry, and Sonya, whose love points him toward confession.
context: It turned the crime story into a journey through conscience and remains one of the great novels of ideas, on morality, freedom and redemption. In Arabic it is best known in Sami al-Droubi's translation of Dostoevsky's complete works.

about: «حكايات غريم» مجموعة يعقوب وويلهلم غريم التي نُشرت أولاً عام 1812، وتُعدّ الأساس الأكاديمي الأول لعلم الفولكلور الغربي. أكثر من مئتي حكاية شعبية ألمانية جمعاها وصنّفاها تشمل سندريلا وسنو وايت وراپونزل والقطة الحيلة وذيب وسبعة جدايات.

الحكايات في صيغتها الأصلية أشد قسوةً مما تعرفه الأجيال الجديدة عبر ديزني: تُقطع الأيدي وتُفقأ الأعين وتُحرق الملكات. الإخوان غريم عدّلوا بعض الحكايات بين الطبعات استجابةً لانتقادات. هذه الحكايات هي الأساس الذي بنت عليه الثقافة الغربية الشعبية صور الأميرة والوحش والساحرة.
context: جمعاها من رواة شفهيين معظمهم كانوا نساءً من البرجوازية الألمانية لا فلاحين. الطبعة السابعة 1857 هي المعتمدة أدبياً.

about: Grimms' Fairy Tales (1812–57) collected over 200 German folk stories — Cinderella, Snow White, Rapunzel, Hansel and Gretel — and created the academic discipline of folklore studies. The original versions are far darker than Disney adaptations: hands severed, eyes gouged out. The foundation of Western popular mythology about witches, princes and enchanted forests.
context: Collected mostly from middle-class women storytellers, not rural peasants. The Brothers revised stories across seven editions. Jacob and Wilhelm were academic linguists, not children's authors — the collection was originally intended for scholars.

about: «الحرب والسلام» رواية ليف تولستوي الملحمية الكبرى، نُشرت بين 1865 و1869، وكثيراً ما تُسمّى أعظم رواية كُتبت في التاريخ. تدور أحداثها بين 1805 و1820 في روسيا القيصرية إبان غزو نابليون لها، وتتابع مصائر خمس عائلات أرستقراطية في خضم الحرب والسلم معاً. الشخصيات الرئيسية أندريه وبيير وناتاشا من أكثر الشخصيات إنسانية وعمقاً في تاريخ الرواية.
تولستوي أراد أن يُثبت أن التاريخ لا يصنعه القادة العظام بل الإرادة الجماعية للشعوب. الرواية خطاب فلسفي مُدمج في ملحمة إنسانية، وهي رغم ضخامتها من أكثر الروايات قراءةً وحباً في العالم.
context: استغرق تولستوي في كتابتها ست سنوات واستعان بزوجته في نسخ المسوّدات مراراً. بعض النقاد يرفضون تصنيفها رواية لأنها تتخطى حدود الجنس الأدبي. نُقلت إلى السينما عدة مرات أشهرها النسخة السوفيتية 1966.

about: War and Peace (1869) follows five aristocratic families through Napoleon's invasion of Russia. Tolstoy's philosophical masterpiece argues that history is made by collective human will, not great leaders. Andrei, Pierre and Natasha are among fiction's most fully realised characters.
context: Took six years to write. Often called the greatest novel ever written, though Tolstoy resisted classifying it as a novel at all. The 1966 Soviet film adaptation won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Film.

about: «الأبله» رواية دوستويفسكي المليئة بالتوتر، نُشرت 1868-1869. بطلها الأمير ميشكين رجل بسيط القلب يحمل شيئاً من نقاء المسيح، يصل إلى بطرسبرغ فيقع بين امرأتين يحبهما: ناستاسيا المعذَّبة وأغلايا الجميلة. نقاوته لا تنقذه في مجتمع فاسد بل تزيد من الكارثة.
دوستويفسكي أراد أن يكتب «الإنسان الطيب الكامل» ليثبت فشل الخير في العالم الحديث. الرواية أكثر أعماله مأساويةً في تصوير الضحية البريئة. نابوكوف الذي أبغض دوستويفسكي أعجب بها رغم ذلك.
context: كتبها في جنيف في فقر شديد وهو يعاني من نوبات الصرع. الرواية تحمل أعمق فهم لمرض الصرع من أي عمل أدبي.

about: The Idiot (1869) follows Prince Myshkin, a Christ-like innocent, into corrupt St Petersburg society where his goodness destroys him and those around him. Dostoevsky's attempt to portray a 'perfectly good man' and its tragic outcome. A devastating portrait of innocence in a fallen world.
context: Written in Geneva while Dostoevsky suffered from epilepsy and poverty. Contains the most profound literary portrayal of epilepsy. Even Nabokov, who disliked Dostoevsky, praised this novel.

about: «الرجل ذو القناع الحديدي» آخر أجزاء رباعية فيكونت دي براجلون لألكسندر دوما، نُشرت 1847-1850. الفصل الختامي يحكي المؤامرة لإنقاذ الأمير السجين الشقيق التوأم للملك لويس الرابع عشر، الذي يخفي وجهه بقناع حديدي في سجن الباستيل. الفرسان الثلاثة الشيوخ يُشاركون في مهمة أخيرة.
دوما أوسع روائي للتاريخ الشعبي وأكثره إمتاعاً. الفصل مؤثر لأنه نهاية أتوس وبورتوس وآراميس وداراتنيان بعد عقود من الروايات. شخصية القناع الحديدي أسطورة تاريخية حقيقية لا يزال لغزها قائماً.
context: القناع الحديدي شخصية حقيقية في التاريخ الفرنسي سُجن في الباستيل دون أن يُعرف اسمه. دوما وسّع حياة دارتنيان عبر ثلاثية ضخمة من أحداث القرن السابع عشر.

about: The Man in the Iron Mask concludes Dumas' Vicomte de Bragelonne trilogy. The aged Three Musketeers make a final attempt to free a mysterious prisoner — the twin brother of Louis XIV — from the Bastille. An emotional farewell to Athos, Porthos, Aramis and d'Artagnan after decades of adventures.
context: The Iron Mask was a real historical prisoner whose identity remains unknown. The scene of Porthos' death is considered one of Dumas' most affecting passages.

about: «كلب آل باسكرفيل» أشهر روايات هولمز الطويلة، نُشرت عام 1902. أسرة باسكرفيل في دفون الإنجليزية تُلاحقها لعنة كلب ضخم يظهر في البرية مع وفاة كل وريث. هولمز وواتسون يحققان في اللغز بين الضباب والمستنقعات.

الرواية تجمع بين الغموض البوليسي والرعب القوطي والمكان الإنجليزي الأثير. الأجواء أكثر مما في أي قصة هولمز أخرى هي المفتاح. واحدة من أكثر الروايات البوليسية مبيعاً في التاريخ وأُخرجت فيلماً عشرات المرات.
context: دويل كتبها بعد «موت» هولمز في شلالات رايخنباخ ليُرضي القراء دون إحيائه رسمياً — ثم أحياه لاحقاً في «العودة». المستنقعات الحقيقية في دارتمور إكزمور ألهمت المكان.

about: The Hound of the Baskervilles (1902) sends Holmes and Watson to fog-shrouded Dartmoor to investigate a supernatural curse — a gigantic hound — haunting the Baskerville family. The Gothic atmosphere and moor setting make it Holmes' most atmospheric case. One of the best-selling detective novels ever written.
context: Written after Holmes' 'death' to satisfy readers without officially reviving him. The real Dartmoor moorlands inspired the setting. Still the most-adapted Holmes story in film and television.

about: «لفياثان» كتاب توماس هوبز الفلسفي الكبير، نُشر عام 1651، وهو الأساس الذي بنت عليه نظرية الدولة الحديثة في الفكر الغربي. هوبز يرى أن الإنسان في الطبيعة يعيش في «حرب الكل ضد الكل»، وأن النظام الاجتماعي يقتضي عقداً اجتماعياً يتنازل فيه الأفراد عن حريتهم لحاكم قوي أو مجلس.

الكتاب أحد ثلاثة كتب أسّست للفكر السياسي الحديث مع لوك وروسو. اسمه مأخوذ من الوحش البحري في التوراة، وهو يصف الدولة بوصفها وحشاً اصطناعياً بُني من الأجساد البشرية. لا تزال حججه حول الأمن والحرية محوراً في الفلسفة السياسية.
context: كتبه هوبز في المنفى الفرنسي أثناء الحرب الأهلية الإنجليزية. حُظر لاحقاً لمحتواه الديني الجريء. لا يزال مقرراً في أقسام الفلسفة والعلوم السياسية.

about: Leviathan (1651) is Thomas Hobbes' founding text of modern political philosophy. Without government, life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short'. His social contract theory — individuals surrender freedom to a powerful sovereign for security — remains central to political thought. Written during the English Civil War.
context: Written in French exile during England's Civil War. The title comes from the biblical sea monster; Hobbes pictures the state as an artificial giant made of human bodies. Required reading in political philosophy alongside Locke and Rousseau.

about: «اعترافات أوغسطينوس» السيرة الروحية لأوغسطينوس الهيبوني، كُتبت نحو 397-400 ميلادي، وهي أولى السير الذاتية الحقيقية في تاريخ الأدب الغربي. أوغسطينوس يحكي سنوات شبابه المتقلب بين الملذات والفلسفة والبحث، حتى يجد طريقه إلى المسيحية بعد صراع طويل.
الكتاب يخاطب الله مباشرةً في خطاب شخصي لا سابق له: «خُلقت لأجلك وقلبي لن يرتاح حتى يستقر فيك». هذا النمط الاعترافي المباشر أسّس لتقليد الكتابة الاعترافية من روسو إلى أدب السير الذاتية الحديث.
context: يُعدّ أول عمل نثري كامل يستخدم الأسلوب الاعترافي في اللغة اللاتينية. أثّر في جميع كتّاب السير الذاتية من روسو إلى كير في رحلاتهم.

about: The Confessions (c.400 CE) by Augustine of Hippo is the first great autobiography in Western literature. Augustine addresses God directly, tracing his restless youth through philosophy and pleasure to Christian faith. 'Our heart is restless until it rests in thee' — one of the most quoted lines in religious writing.
context: The first sustained first-person confessional narrative in Latin prose. Its influence on all subsequent autobiography — Rousseau, Tolstoy, modern memoir — is incalculable.

about: «يوليسيس» رواية جيمس جويس، نُشرت عام 1922، وتُعدّ من أعظم وأصعب الروايات في القرن العشرين. تحكي يوماً واحداً 16 يونيو 1904 في دبلن عبر تيار وعي ليوبولد بلوم وزوجته مولي وستيفن ديدالس. كل فصل مكتوب بأسلوب مختلف.

الرواية استكشاف جذري لإمكانيات اللغة الروائية: لا قصة خطية، بل تداعيات وأفكار وحوار داخلي. مونولوغ مولي بلوم الختامي الذي يمتد لعشرات الصفحات دون علامات ترقيم من أجرأ ما كُتب في الأدب. تحتاج إلى دليل قراءة لكنها تُكافئ القارئ الصابر.
context: نُشرت في باريس لأن أمريكا ومعظم بلدان الأنجلوفون حظرتها لسنوات. لا تزال في قوائم أعظم عشر روايات في معظم الاستطلاعات الأدبية.

about: Ulysses (1922) follows Leopold Bloom through a single day in Dublin using stream-of-consciousness narration across eighteen episodes each written in a different style. Molly Bloom's final soliloquy — unpunctuated for pages — is one of literature's boldest experiments. Requires a guide; rewards patient readers enormously.
context: Published in Paris; banned in the US and UK for years on obscenity grounds. Consistently tops lists of the greatest novels in English. Joyce mapped the day in minute detail using a real Dublin 16 June 1904, still celebrated as 'Bloomsday'.

about: «ما وراء الخير والشر» كتاب فريدريك نيتشه، نُشر عام 1886، وهو من أعمق نقوداته للفلسفة الأخلاقية الغربية. يهاجم نيتشه الفلسفة الكانطية والأخلاق المسيحية وفكرة الحقيقة المطلقة، ويؤسس لما سمّاه «فلسفة المستقبل» التي تتجاوز ثنائية الخير والشر.
نيتشه يكتب بشكل متكسر: أمثال وحكم وسخرية ولا أطروحات طويلة. كتاب مثير للإشكالية والجدل وقد قُرئ خطأً وصواباً، لكنه يبقى من أكثر كتب الفلسفة تأثيراً في القرن العشرين بلا منازع.
context: يكمل ما بدأه في «إنسان أكثر إنسانية». أسيء تفسيره فاشياً من قِبَل أخته إليزابيث بعد وفاته. نيتشه نفسه كان معادياً للعنصرية والقومية الألمانية بشكل صريح.

about: Beyond Good and Evil (1886) attacks Kantian ethics, Christian morality and the concept of objective truth. Nietzsche proposes that moral systems are merely expressions of will to power and calls for a 'philosophy of the future'. Written in aphorisms and withering irony. Among the most influential and misread works in Western philosophy.
context: Misappropriated by Nietzsche's sister as proto-Nazi philosophy after his death. Nietzsche himself was explicitly anti-nationalist and anti-antisemitic. Read properly, it is a radical call for intellectual honesty and self-overcoming.

about: «المسخ» قصة كافكا القصيرة الأشهر، نُشرت عام 1915. غريغور سامسا يستيقظ ذات صباح فيجد نفسه تحوّل إلى حشرة ضخمة. لكن المأساة الحقيقية ليست التحول بل ردة فعل عائلته التي تنتقل من الذهول إلى الإحراج إلى الإهمال إلى التخلص.
في عشرة آلاف كلمة تقريباً يقول كافكا ما لم يقله غيره: الفرد وسط الأسرة، وكيف يصبح المريض أو العاجز عبئاً يتحول الاهتمام به إلى كراهية. لا تزال من أكثر النصوص القصيرة قراءةً ودراسةً في العالم.
context: كافكا كتبها في ثلاثة أسابيع. قال محررون كثيرون إن الغلاف يجب ألا يُظهر الحشرة بصورة حرفية.

about: The Metamorphosis (1915) opens with Gregor Samsa waking to find himself transformed into a giant insect. His family's reaction — from shock to embarrassment to relief at his death — is the true horror. In under a hundred pages, Kafka captures the human cost of uselessness and the thin line between love and convenience.
context: Written in three weeks. Kafka insisted no illustration of the insect appear on the cover — the power lies in not knowing exactly what Gregor has become. Among the most-taught short texts in world literature.

about: «الرجل الخفي» رواية ويلز، نُشرت عام 1897. عالم مجنون يكتشف طريقة لجعل جسده شفافاً تماماً، لكن عجزه عن العودة إلى المرئية يحوّله من مجرب علمي إلى مجرم مطارَد. الرواية استعارة عميقة عن العبقرية حين تُفقد الرادع الأخلاقي.

ويلز يُظهر أن الاختفاء بدلاً من أن يمنح الحرية يُؤدي إلى العزل الكامل: لا يمكنك أن تأكل في العلن، ولا أن تدفأ، ولا أن تُحَبّ. القوة المطلقة بدون جذور إنسانية تُدمّر صاحبها. ولا تزال الرواية أساساً لأفلام عديدة عن الاختفاء.
context: كتبها بعد نجاح «آلة الزمن» وتُكمّل اهتمامه بنتائج العلم خارج حدود الأخلاق. لا تزال مرجعاً في أفلام الخيال العلمي حتى اليوم.

about: The Invisible Man (1897) follows a scientist who makes himself invisible but cannot reverse the process. Hunted and isolated, his genius turns to crime. Wells shows that invisibility means total disconnection from humanity — power without moral grounding destroys its possessor.
context: Written after the success of The Time Machine. One of the earliest science fiction works to explore the ethical consequences of scientific discovery rather than just its wonders.

about: «هكذا تحدث زرادشت» أشهر كتب نيتشه وأكثرها شعريةً، نُشر في أجزاء بين 1883 و1885. زرادشت النبي الفيلسوف ينزل من جبله بعد عشر سنين من العزلة ليعلّم الناس «الإنسان الأعلى» وفكرة «الإرادة للقوة» و«العود الأبدي».

كتبه نيتشه بلغة شعرية تُذكّر بالكتاب المقدس ليقول بالضبط عكس ما يقوله. جملته «الله مات» ليست إعلاناً بهيجاً بل تشخيص لأزمة المعنى في الحداثة. الكتاب أثّر في ماهلر وريلكه وهسه وسرت مسيرة الوجودية كلها.
context: نيتشه نفسه اعتبره أعظم ما كتب. كُشف عن تفاصيل الطبعة في رسائله كأنه يتحدث عن إنجاز روحي. أسيء استخدامه نازياً وهو بريء من ذلك تماماً.

about: Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883–85) presents Nietzsche's prophet descending from a mountain to teach the Übermensch, eternal recurrence and will to power. Written in a poetic, Bible-like style that deliberately inverts its model. 'God is dead' is not celebration but diagnosis of modernity's crisis of meaning. Influenced Mahler, Rilke, Hesse and existentialism.
context: Nietzsche considered it his greatest work. Misappropriated by Nazis despite being explicitly anti-nationalist. Its poetic ambition makes it both his most inspiring and most misread text.

about: «المحاكمة» رواية فرانز كافكا، كُتبت عام 1914 ونُشرت بعد وفاته عام 1925 بإذن مخالف لوصيته. يوزف كاف يستيقظ صباحاً ليجد نفسه مُعتقلاً بتهمة لا يعلمها أحد، ويخضع لمحاكمة لا يعرف قواعدها ولا ممثليها. الرواية معجزة في بناء شعور القلق الوجودي دون تسميته.
«كافكاوي» كلمة باتت في اللغات العالمية تصف البيروقراطية العبثية والشعور بالاتهام دون ذنب. الرواية استعارة للحداثة والدولة الشمولية وللشعور الإنساني بأنك في مواجهة نظام أكبر منك بلا معنى.
context: كافكا طلب إحراق مخطوطاته لكن صديقه ماكس برود نشرها. الرواية أحد أكثر النصوص تأثيراً في الأدب الوجودي والتيار اللاهوتي الحديث.

about: The Trial (published 1925) follows Josef K., arrested one morning on charges no one will explain, tried by a court whose rules no one knows. Kafka's masterwork of existential dread. The word 'Kafkaesque' entered the language to describe its atmosphere of absurd, faceless bureaucratic power.
context: Kafka ordered it burned; his friend Max Brod published it. Profoundly influenced existentialism, absurdism and every writer who came after. The unfinished state of the novel adds to rather than detracts from its unsettling power.

about: «الكوميديا الإلهية» ملحمة دانتي أليغييري الشعرية، كُتبت بين 1308 و1320، وهي أعظم ما أنتجته آداب العصور الوسطى الأوروبية. دانتي يُرافقه الشاعر فيرجيل في رحلة عبر الجحيم والمطهر، ثم ترافقه بياتريتشي في الجنة. الجحيم «الإنفيرنو» أشهر الأقسام الثلاثة.

القصيدة خريطة اللاهوت الكاثوليكي الوسيط وفيها شخصيات تاريخية وأساطيرية. لكنها كذلك قصيدة سياسية شخصية: دانتي المنفي من فلورنسا يضع خصومه في الجحيم وأصدقاءه في الجنة. صاغت المفهوم الغربي عن الثواب والعقاب في الحياة الآخرة لقرون.
context: كتبها بالإيطالية لا باللاتينية مما رسّخ الإيطالية لغةً أدبية. مليئة بالإشارات إلى شخصيات تاريخية ودينية تستحق قراءتها مع شرح.

about: The Divine Comedy (1308–20) by Dante Alighieri is a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Heaven guided by Virgil then Beatrice. The Inferno with its vivid circles of punishment is the most famous section. Written in Italian, it shaped Western ideas of the afterlife and established Italian as a literary language.
context: Dante placed real political enemies in Hell and friends in Heaven, making it a coded political manifesto as much as a spiritual vision. Essential reading with commentary due to its dense classical and biblical references.

about: «بيوولف» أقدم ملحمة شعرية إنجليزية، كُتبت بالإنجليزية القديمة نحو القرن الثامن أو العاشر الميلادي ويمتد عمر أحداثها إلى القرن السادس. البطل الجرماني بيوولف يحارب الوحش غرنديل ثم أمه ثم تنيناً في شيخوخته. الملحمة جمعت الأساطير الجرمانية القديمة بالبعد الديني المسيحي.

للملحمة أهمية تأسيسية في الأدب الإنجليزي: هي أول نص شعري طويل محفوظ في اللغة الإنجليزية. ترجمها شيموس هيني الشاعر الإيرلندي الحائز نوبل عام 1999 بأسلوب أضاء جمالها من جديد. تولكين كتب عنها مقالاً مؤثراً عام 1936 قلب تقييمها الأكاديمي.
context: المخطوطة الوحيدة الناجية محفوظة في المتحف البريطاني. مقال تولكين «بيوولف: الوحوش والنقاد» أعاد الاهتمام بها أدبياً لا تاريخياً.

about: Beowulf, the oldest surviving long poem in English (composed c.700–1000 CE), follows the Geat warrior Beowulf as he defeats the monster Grendel, then Grendel's mother, then a dragon in old age. The fusion of pagan heroic tradition with Christian themes created a unique and haunting work. Seamus Heaney's 1999 translation renewed its reputation.
context: The single surviving manuscript is in the British Library. Tolkien's 1936 essay 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics' transformed its scholarly reception, arguing it should be read as a poem, not just a historical document.

about: «الإخوة كارامازوف» آخر وأعظم روايات دوستويفسكي، نُشرت 1879-1880 قُبيل وفاته بأشهر. تدور حول عائلة كارامازوف الروسية المفككة: الأب المستهتر فيودور والأبناء الثلاثة المتناقضون: الشهواني ديمتري والمثقف الشاك إيفان والراهب القديس أليوشا. حين يُقتل الأب تُطرح على الجميع أسئلة الذنب والمسؤولية والإيمان.
الرواية أعمق استكشاف فلسفي عرفه الأدب لأسئلة وجود الله والشر والحرية. مقطع «قضية المحقق الكبير» الذي يرويه إيفان من أهم النصوص الفلسفية في الأدب العالمي. قال عنها فرويد إنها أعظم رواية كُتبت قط.
context: كتبها دوستويفسكي يريدها الجزء الأول من ثلاثية لم يُكمّلها بسبب وفاته. أثّرت في فرويد وكافكا وغاندي وكثير من المفكرين في القرن العشرين.

about: The Brothers Karamazov (1880) is Dostoevsky's final and greatest novel: a family saga, murder mystery and philosophical inquiry into God, free will and suffering. Ivan's 'Grand Inquisitor' chapter is one of literature's greatest philosophical set-pieces. Freud called it the greatest novel ever written.
context: Intended as the first part of an unfinished trilogy. Influenced Freud, Kafka and Gandhi. Dostoevsky died four months after its completion.

about: «ليالٍ بيضاء» قصة دوستويفسكي القصيرة الأكثر شاعريةً، نُشرت عام 1848. في أربع ليالٍ خلال ظاهرة «الليالي البيضاء» التي تطول فيها أيام بطرسبرغ الصيفية، يلتقي الراوي العاطفي المنعزل بالفتاة ناستنكا التي تنتظر محبوبها الغائب. يقع في حبها بينما قلبها مع آخر.
القصة تختلف عن سائر أعمال دوستويفسكي في لطفها ورقتها. هي رثاء للأحلام التي لا تتحقق وللوحيد الذي يعطي دون أن يأخذ. قصيدة سردية أكثر من قصة، وقد ألهمت أفلاماً متعددة منها فيلم فيسكونتي الإيطالي 1957.
context: مع أنها مبكرة في مسيرة دوستويفسكي فإنها تُقرأ كتمرين فيه أبرز سمات أسلوبه من حضور المدينة وعمق الحياة الداخلية.

about: White Nights (1848) is Dostoevsky's most lyrical short work. During St Petersburg's midnight-sun summer nights, a lonely dreamer falls for a girl waiting for a man who may never return. A tender, melancholic poem in prose about unrequited love and solitude.
context: An early work but already distinctly Dostoevsky's. Inspired Luchino Visconti's 1957 film. One of literature's most affecting short meditations on loneliness.

about: أشهر كتب جبران خليل جبران، كتبه بالإنجليزية ونشره عام 1923. يستعد الحكيم المصطفى لركوب السفينة التي جاءت تعيده إلى بلده بعد اثنتي عشرة سنة قضاها في مدينة أورفليس، فيجتمع حوله أهلها ويسألونه عن الحب والزواج والأبناء والعمل والفرح والحزن والحرية والموت، فيجيبهم في فصول قصيرة من النثر الشعري.
context: تُرجم «النبي» إلى عشرات اللغات، وصار من أكثر الكتب مبيعاً في القرن العشرين، وما زالت فقراته تُقرأ في الأعراس والمناسبات حول العالم، مثل قوله عن الأبناء: «أولادكم ليسوا أولاداً لكم». وله ترجمات عربية كثيرة، منها ترجمة أنطونيوس بشير وترجمة ميخائيل نعيمة.
والكتاب قصير يُقرأ في ساعة، لكن كثيرين يعودون إليه مرات كثيرة في حياتهم.

about: Gibran's most famous book, written in English and published in 1923. As the sage Almustafa prepares to board the ship that will take him home after twelve years in the city of Orphalese, its people ask him about love, marriage, children, work, joy and sorrow, freedom and death, and he answers in short chapters of poetic prose.
context: Translated into dozens of languages and one of the best-selling books of the twentieth century, it is still read aloud at weddings and funerals; its line 'Your children are not your children' is quoted around the world.

about: «المجنون» أول كتاب كتبه جبران خليل جبران بالإنجليزية، ونُشر في نيويورك عام 1918، وهو مجموعة من الأمثال والقصائد النثرية القصيرة. في القطعة الأولى يستيقظ رجل فيجد أن أقنعته كلها قد سُرقت، فيركض في الشوارع عاري الوجه، وحين تقبّل الشمس وجهه للمرة الأولى يصير «المجنون» الذي يحمل الكتاب اسمه: حرّاً ووحيداً. وما بعدها حكايات قصيرة ساخرة ومُرّة أحياناً عن النفاق والكبرياء والعزلة.
context: زيّن جبران الكتاب برسومه، وهو أشدّ قتامة وحدّة من [النبي](/book/98) الذي جاء بعده بخمس سنوات، وفيه نرى جبران يجد صوت الحكيم الغريب الذي اشتهر به. ومعظم القطع لا تتجاوز صفحة واحدة، فهو كتاب يُقرأ على مهل، قطعةً قطعة.

about: Gibran's first book written in English, published in 1918, is a collection of short parables and prose poems. In the opening piece a man discovers that his masks have been stolen; as he runs through the streets bare-faced, the sun kisses his face for the first time, and he becomes the madman of the title, free and alone. The tales that follow are brief, ironic and often bitter, about hypocrisy, pride and loneliness.
context: Illustrated with Gibran's own drawings, The Madman is darker and sharper than [The Prophet](/book/98?lang=en), which came five years later, and it shows him finding the voice of the wise outsider that made him famous. Most pieces are only a page long, so it is an easy book to dip into.

about: Makar Devushkin is a middle-aged copying clerk who can barely afford his corner behind a kitchen partition, and Varvara Dobroselova is a young orphan living across the courtyard. They write to each other almost daily, and in their letters they share sweets, worries, borrowed books and small lies about how well they are managing. Makar spends money he does not have to keep her comfortable, while Varvara quietly watches her options run out.
context: This was Dostoevsky's first novel, published in 1846 when he was twenty-four, and its success was immediate: the critic Belinsky received it with enthusiasm, and literary Petersburg spoke of a new Gogol. It is gentler than his later books, but the dignity of poor people and the shame of being pitied are already his subjects. Read it beside [White Nights](/book/17?lang=en) for the early Dostoevsky.

about: A nobleman named Goryanchikov serves ten years in a Siberian prison camp for killing his wife, and his notes describe the place from the inside: the shackles, the bathhouse on a feast day, the prisoners' theatre, the floggings, the eagle the convicts keep and then set free. Instead of a plot there is a crowd of characters, smugglers, murderers, Old Believers, all observed without sermon and often with surprising warmth.
context: Behind the fictional narrator stands Dostoevsky's own four years of hard labour in Omsk after his mock execution in 1849. Tolstoy rated this book among the best in Russian literature, and its question of what remains human in people the law has written off runs straight into [Crime and Punishment](/book/12?lang=en).

about: Published abroad in 1894 because the Russian censors banned it, this is Tolstoy's long argument that the Sermon on the Mount should be taken literally: do not resist evil with violence. He goes through the churches, the armies and the courts and asks how a Christian state can draft men to kill, collect taxes for war and imprison its critics, and answers that it cannot.
context: The young lawyer Mohandas Gandhi read it in South Africa and later said it overwhelmed him; the two men exchanged letters in 1909 and 1910. If you know Tolstoy only from [War and Peace](/book/21?lang=en), this book shows the moralist he became in his later years, blunt, stubborn and impossible to ignore.

about: Gilliatt is a solitary fisherman on the island of Guernsey whom his neighbours suspect of witchcraft. When the steamship Durande is wrecked on the Douvres rocks, its owner promises his niece Déruchette to whoever can bring the engine back. Gilliatt goes out alone and spends weeks on the reef, fighting storms, hunger and, in the most famous scene, a giant octopus.
context: Hugo wrote the novel in 1866 during his exile on Guernsey and dedicated it to the island. It is a story of human will against the sea, and its ending is one of the most quietly heartbreaking he wrote. Readers who loved the scale of [Les Misérables](/book/44?lang=en) will find here a smaller, wilder book.

about: In the London of 1547, two boys born on the same day meet by chance: Tom Canty, a beggar's son from Offal Court, and Prince Edward, heir to Henry VIII. They swap clothes for fun, the guards throw the real prince out of the palace, and each must survive in the other's world. Edward learns how harsh his father's laws are for the poor, while Tom discovers the absurd rituals of the court.
context: Published in 1881, it was Mark Twain's first historical novel, and it is often given to young readers, but beneath the comedy is a sharp attack on cruel punishments and inherited privilege. It makes a good companion to [A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court](/book/51?lang=en), his other trip into the English past.

about: Hank Morgan, a practical superintendent from a Hartford arms factory, is knocked out in a fight and wakes up in Camelot in the year 528. About to be burned at the stake, he remembers a solar eclipse and passes himself off as a magician. Soon he is building factories, newspapers and telephone lines, and duelling knights with a lasso, determined to drag the sixth century into the nineteenth.
context: Published in 1889, the book is part comic fantasy and part angry satire of chivalry, slavery and the power of an established church, and its ending turns surprisingly dark. It was also one of the first time-travel stories, appearing six years before [The Time Machine](/book/179?lang=en).

about: In 1867 Mark Twain joined a group of American tourists aboard the steamship Quaker City for a five-month tour of Europe, Egypt and the Holy Land, sending letters to newspapers along the way. This book collects and reworks them: Paris and the Italian galleries, the Sphinx, Constantinople, the long ride through Palestine, and everywhere the pious, guidebook-quoting passengers he calls the pilgrims.
context: It was Twain's best-selling book during his lifetime. Its pleasure lies in his refusal to admire what he is told to admire, and in the honesty with which he describes being tired, bored or moved. Travel writing changed after it, and it still reads fresher than most modern travel guides.

about: Before he was a writer, Samuel Clemens learned to pilot steamboats on the Mississippi, and the first half of this book tells how a cocky young cub was taught by the pilot Horace Bixby to read every bend, snag and shallow of twelve hundred miles of river. In the second half he returns in 1882, after the Civil War and the railways have changed everything, and travels the river again.
context: The book even explains his pen name: 'mark twain' was the leadsman's call for two fathoms of water, safe depth for a boat. It is the best background to [Adventures of Huckleberry Finn](/book/49?lang=en) and [The Adventures of Tom Sawyer](/book/48?lang=en), and a portrait of a world that disappeared within one man's lifetime.

about: The second collection of Sherlock Holmes stories, published in 1894, holds some of the best: 'Silver Blaze', with its curious incident of the dog in the night-time, 'The Gloria Scott' and 'The Musgrave Ritual', cases from before Holmes met Watson, and 'The Greek Interpreter', which introduces his cleverer and lazier brother Mycroft.
context: It ends with 'The Final Problem', in which Conan Doyle, tired of his detective, sent him over the Reichenbach Falls with Professor Moriarty. Readers were outraged, and the story of how Holmes came back is told in [The Return of Sherlock Holmes](/book/59?lang=en). Start with [The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes](/book/54?lang=en) if you are new to the series.

about: A coded warning from an informer inside Professor Moriarty's organisation reaches Baker Street too late: a man named John Douglas has been found shot in his moated manor house at Birlstone. Holmes and Watson investigate a locked-room puzzle full of strange details, a missing dumbbell, a wedding ring taken from the victim's finger, and a card bearing the letters V.V. 341.
context: Published in 1915, this is the last of the four Holmes novels. Like [A Study in Scarlet](/book/56?lang=en), it moves halfway through to America, here to the coal valleys of Pennsylvania and a secret society inspired by the real Molly Maguires, with a tense undercover story that many readers think the best part of the book.

about: Professor Challenger, a brilliant and violent zoologist, claims he has seen living prehistoric animals on an isolated plateau in the Amazon. To prove it he leads an expedition with a sceptical rival, a big-game hunter and the young journalist Edward Malone, who has joined only to impress the woman he loves. On the plateau they find dinosaurs, pterodactyls and a war between ape-men and an Indigenous people.
context: Published in 1912, The Lost World created the modern adventure of the hidden land of dinosaurs, and everything from King Kong to Jurassic Park owes it something. Challenger's bad temper and Malone's light humour make it great fun, especially for readers of Jules Verne such as [Five Weeks in a Balloon](/book/126?lang=en).

about: Sir Robert Chiltern is a rising politician with a perfect reputation and a wife who adores him for it. Then the elegant Mrs Cheveley arrives with a letter proving that he made his fortune by selling a state secret as a young man, and she demands his help with a fraudulent canal scheme. The only person who can save him is his friend Lord Goring, an idle dandy who turns out to be the wisest man in the play.
context: First staged in January 1895, the play mixes Wilde's famous wit with a serious question: should we love people for being perfect, or forgive them for not being? It pairs naturally with [The Importance of Being Earnest](/book/63?lang=en), which opened a few weeks later.

about: On a terrace of Herod's palace, the princess Salomé hears the voice of the prophet Jokanaan (John the Baptist) from the cistern where he is kept prisoner. She falls in love with him, he rejects her, and when Herod begs her to dance for him she agrees, on one condition: the prophet's head on a silver platter.
context: Wilde wrote the play in French in 1891. Its London production was banned in rehearsal because it showed biblical characters, and it was first staged in Paris in 1896 while Wilde was in prison. Aubrey Beardsley's illustrations for the English edition and Richard Strauss's opera made it one of the defining works of the decadent era.

about: Five fairy tales: the gilded statue of the Happy Prince, who asks a swallow to strip away his gold and jewels for the poor of his city; the nightingale who gives her life to make a red rose for a student; the Selfish Giant whose garden stays in winter until he lets the children in; and two sharp comic tales, 'The Devoted Friend' and 'The Remarkable Rocket'.
context: Published in 1888, when Wilde's two sons were small, these stories are as beautiful read aloud to children as they are sad to adults. They belong on the same shelf as [Andersen's tales](/book/192?lang=en), and they show a tender side of the writer best known for his epigrams.

about: Written in Reading Gaol in the first months of 1897, De Profundis is a very long letter from Oscar Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas, the young man whose quarrel with his father led to Wilde's trial and two years' hard labour. It begins as a bitter account of their friendship, then becomes a meditation on suffering, humility, art and the figure of Christ.
context: The title comes from Psalm 130, 'Out of the depths'. A shortened version appeared in 1905, after Wilde's death, and the full text was only published in 1962. It is the most personal thing Wilde wrote, and reading it after [The Picture of Dorian Gray](/book/62?lang=en) is a startling experience.

about: At a dinner party in Athens to celebrate the poet Agathon's victory in a drama contest, the guests agree to drink lightly and instead give speeches in praise of Love. The doctor, the poet and the comic playwright Aristophanes, with his myth of humans split in two and searching for their other halves, all speak before Socrates, who repeats what a wise woman named Diotima taught him about love as a ladder rising toward beauty itself.
context: Then the drunk Alcibiades bursts in and gives a wild, funny, painful speech about Socrates himself. The dialogue gave us the idea of Platonic love and is the most dramatic and best-loved of Plato's works; read it with [Phaedrus](/book/78?lang=en), his other great dialogue on love.

about: On the last day of his life, Socrates sits in prison with his friends and talks calmly about whether the soul survives death. He offers one argument after another, from opposites, from recollection, from the soul's likeness to unchanging things, while his friends raise objections he takes seriously. At sunset he drinks the hemlock, and the account of his death is among the most moving pages in ancient literature.
context: Narrated by Phaedo, who was in the cell, the dialogue completes the story begun in the [Apology](/book/75?lang=en) and [Crito](/book/82?lang=en). It shaped centuries of thinking about the soul, in the Islamic world as well as in Europe, and it is a fine introduction to Plato's theory of Forms.

about: Socrates and the young Phaedrus walk out of Athens and sit under a plane tree by the river Ilissus, where Phaedrus reads him a clever speech on love by the orator Lysias. Socrates answers with two speeches of his own, and in the second compares the soul to a charioteer driving two winged horses, one noble and one unruly.
context: The second half turns to rhetoric and writing. Socrates tells the Egyptian myth of the god who invented letters and the king who warned that writing would weaken memory, an argument that sounds surprisingly modern in the age of screens. It is one of Plato's most beautiful dialogues and a natural partner to the [Symposium](/book/76?lang=en).

about: Timaeus, an astronomer from southern Italy, explains how the universe came to be: a divine craftsman, looking to eternal patterns, shaped the world as a living, ordered body with a soul. He builds the elements out of geometric shapes, describes time as a moving image of eternity, and goes on to the human body and its diseases. The introduction also tells, for the first time, the story of lost Atlantis.
context: For more than a thousand years this was the dialogue of Plato that medieval Europe knew best, through a Latin translation, and it shaped the medieval picture of the cosmos. It is hard going in places, but read slowly, it shows philosophy and science before they became separate subjects.

about: Meno, a confident young aristocrat, asks Socrates whether virtue can be taught, and within a few pages discovers that he cannot even say what virtue is. To answer the puzzle of how we can look for something we do not know, Socrates calls over a slave boy who has never studied geometry and, by questions alone, leads him to work out how to double the area of a square.
context: The demonstration supports Plato's idea that learning is recollection, and the dialogue is one of the shortest and clearest ways into his thought. Watch for Anytus, who appears briefly and leaves with a threat: he would later be one of Socrates' accusers, as the [Apology](/book/75?lang=en) tells.

about: It is just before dawn in the prison, and Socrates' old friend Crito has bribed the guards: everything is ready for an escape. Socrates listens, then asks whether it would be right to break the law, even an unjust verdict. He imagines the Laws of Athens speaking to him, reminding him of everything he owes them, and decides to stay.
context: The Crito is very short and can be read in half an hour, but its question about duty to the state and the limits of obedience has never gone away. It sits between the trial in the [Apology](/book/75?lang=en) and the death scene in the [Phaedo](/book/77?lang=en).

about: Aristotle begins from the household and the village and ends with the best possible state, arguing that human beings are by nature political animals who can only live well in a community. He collects and compares the constitutions of Greek cities, sorts governments into good forms and their corrupt twins, criticises Plato's ideal city and recommends a large middle class as the surest foundation of stability.
context: Some of it, especially his defence of slavery, is hard to read today, and some of it reads like modern political science. Curiously, the Politics was not translated into Arabic in the Middle Ages, which is why Ibn Rushd wrote his commentary on Plato's [Republic](/book/74?lang=en) instead.

about: After ten years alone on a mountain, the prophet Zarathustra comes down to share what he has learned and finds the people laughing at him. In a series of parables, songs and speeches, Nietzsche has him announce the death of God, the coming of the Übermensch who will create new values, and the dizzying thought of eternal recurrence, the idea that every moment of life will return forever.
context: Written between 1883 and 1885 in a deliberately biblical style, it is Nietzsche's most poetic book and the one he valued most. Richard Strauss turned it into a tone poem whose opening became famous in the film 2001. Read it slowly, a few chapters at a time, as you would read poetry.

about: Nietzsche's first book, published in 1872 when he was a young professor of classics, asks how the cheerful Greeks came to invent tragedy. His answer is a struggle between two forces he names after gods: Apollo, who stands for form, order and the beautiful image, and Dionysus, who stands for intoxication, music and the dissolving of the self. Greek tragedy, he says, was born when the two were held together.
context: He also blames Socrates and Euripides for killing tragedy with reason, and ends by hailing Wagner's music as its rebirth. Classical scholars attacked the book harshly, but the Apollonian and the Dionysian became lasting terms for thinking about art. The later preface, in which Nietzsche criticises his own youthful book, is worth reading first.

about: Written in 1888 and held back until 1895, The Antichrist is Nietzsche's direct attack on Christianity, which he accuses of turning weakness into a virtue and teaching people to despise life in this world. It is short, furious and often deliberately offensive, yet it also draws a striking line between the figure of Jesus and the church that Paul built in his name.
context: Read it as a document of Nietzsche's last productive year rather than as a balanced argument; its force comes from its anger. The book is easier to understand after [Beyond Good and Evil](/book/92?lang=en), where his ideas about master and slave morality are worked out more patiently.

about: In the autumn of 1888, shortly before his mental collapse in Turin, Nietzsche wrote this short autobiography with chapters called 'Why I Am So Wise', 'Why I Am So Clever' and 'Why I Write Such Good Books'. He looks back on his illnesses, his diet, his love of music and each of his books in turn, and ends by declaring that he is a destiny.
context: The title is Pilate's phrase 'Behold the man'. The tone swings between brilliance, humour and unsettling grandiosity, and the book was only published in 1908. It is the best map of his work by its own author, so it is worth reading after one or two of his other books.

about: Dr Samuel Fergusson, his reluctant friend Dick Kennedy, a hunter, and his cheerful servant Joe set out from Zanzibar to cross Africa from east to west in a hydrogen balloon called the Victoria. Fergusson has invented a way to rise and fall by heating the gas, so they can float on the winds over deserts, lakes and the then-unknown sources of the Nile.
context: Published in 1863, this was Jules Verne's first novel and the start of his long partnership with the publisher Hetzel. The geography reflects European knowledge and attitudes of its time, but the mix of adventure and real science is already pure Verne, leading on to [Around the World in Eighty Days](/book/122?lang=en).

about: In 1625 young d'Artagnan rides from Gascony to Paris with a letter of introduction, an old horse and a hot temper, and on his first day challenges three of the King's Musketeers to duels: Athos, Porthos and Aramis. Instead of fighting they become friends, and together they race to England to recover the Queen's diamond studs before Cardinal Richelieu and the beautiful, deadly Milady de Winter can ruin her.
context: Serialised in a Paris newspaper in 1844 and written with Auguste Maquet, the novel gave the world 'all for one, one for all'. It is pure narrative pleasure, and the adventures continue in [Twenty Years After](/book/135?lang=en) and [The Man in the Iron Mask](/book/134?lang=en).

about: Twenty years on, the friends have scattered: Athos lives as a country gentleman, Porthos is rich and bored, Aramis has become an abbé, and d'Artagnan is still a lieutenant. France is torn by the uprising of the Fronde, and Cardinal Mazarin needs men he can trust. The four find themselves on opposite sides, then reunite to attempt something desperate, saving King Charles I of England from the scaffold.
context: Published in 1845, the sequel is darker than [The Three Musketeers](/book/133?lang=en): the heroes are older, history is crueller, and Mordaunt, the son of Milady, has come for revenge. Many readers think it is the best book of the trilogy.

about: In The Hague in 1672, a furious crowd murders the brothers Johan and Cornelius de Witt, the leaders of the Dutch republic. Cornelius's godson, a gentle tulip grower named Cornelius van Baerle, is drawn into the affair through a packet of letters left in his care, just as he is close to breeding a pure black tulip, the flower that would win a fortune from the growers of Haarlem.
context: Imprisoned in the fortress of Loevestein, he finds help in Rosa, the jailer's daughter, and the novel becomes a love story built around a single bulb. Published in 1850, it is shorter and quieter than [The Three Musketeers](/book/133?lang=en), and it opens with a powerful scene of real historical violence.

about: In the late twenty-first century England has become a republic, and its narrator, Lionel Verney, tells the story of his friends, a romantic poet-lord and a gentle idealist, as they struggle with war and politics. Then a plague appears in the East and spreads across the world, and Verney watches the human race shrink, nation by nation, until he may be the only one left.
context: Published in 1826, eight years after [Frankenstein](/book/137?lang=en), the novel was poorly received and largely forgotten until the twentieth century. It is now read as one of the first great pandemic novels and as Mary Shelley's grieving portrait of Percy Shelley and Lord Byron, both of whom had recently died.

about: A Wall Street lawyer hires a pale, quiet copyist named Bartleby, who at first works tirelessly. Then one day, asked to check a document, Bartleby replies, 'I would prefer not to.' Soon he prefers not to do anything at all, and not to leave the office either, and the narrator's kindness, anger and guilt cannot move him.
context: First published in a magazine in 1853, this long short story is funny, sad and strange, and every generation reads it differently: as a story about office work, depression, protest or the limits of charity. It is a good way to discover Melville before tackling [Moby-Dick](/book/141?lang=en).

about: In 1842 a young American sailor deserts his whaling ship in the Marquesas Islands with a friend and, after a hard trek over the mountains, ends up in the valley of the Typee people, who are feared as cannibals. He is treated as an honoured guest, nursed through an injured leg and shown a life of ease and beauty, yet he is never allowed to leave.
context: Typee was Herman Melville's first book, based on his own weeks in the Marquesas, and it made him famous in 1846 as the man who had lived among the cannibals. Its criticism of missionaries and colonial powers was bold for its time, and its love of the sea leads directly to [Moby-Dick](/book/141?lang=en).

about: In 1797, months after mutinies shook the British navy, the young sailor Billy Budd is taken from a merchant ship to serve on a warship. Everyone loves him for his beauty and innocence except the master-at-arms, John Claggart, who falsely accuses him of plotting mutiny. Billy, who stammers when upset, cannot answer in words and strikes Claggart dead, and Captain Vere must decide his fate.
context: Melville was still revising this short novel when he died in 1891, and it was not published until 1924. It is a moral puzzle about law, justice and conscience, and it became an opera by Benjamin Britten. Read it after [Bartleby, the Scrivener](/book/142?lang=en) for Melville's late, quieter style.

about: Twelve years after On the Origin of Species, Darwin addressed the question his first book had carefully avoided: where human beings come from. He argues that we descend from earlier primates, traces our mental and moral faculties to animal origins, and suggests Africa as the probable cradle of humanity. Much of the book is about sexual selection, the competition for mates that explains the peacock's tail and the songs of birds.
context: Published in 1871, it caused as much debate as the Origin, and some of its views on race and on women belong very much to Victorian England. Its central arguments, however, still shape biology. Read it with [On the Origin of Species](/book/145?lang=en) and [The Expression of the Emotions](/book/148?lang=en).

about: In 1831 a twenty-two-year-old Charles Darwin sailed from Plymouth on HMS Beagle as the captain's gentleman companion, and spent nearly five years exploring South America, the Galápagos Islands, Tahiti, New Zealand and Australia. His journal records it all: fossils of giant extinct mammals, an earthquake in Chile, the people of Tierra del Fuego and the strange birds and tortoises of the Galápagos.
context: First published in 1839, this was the book that made Darwin known, and it is far more readable than his scientific works: an adventure told by a curious young man. The observations he made here led, twenty years later, to [On the Origin of Species](/book/145?lang=en).

about: Why do people from different cultures smile, frown and blush in the same way? Darwin collected answers from missionaries around the world, observed the faces of his own children and studied animals in the London zoo to show that many expressions are inherited, shared with other animals and older than language.
context: Published in 1872, it was one of the first scientific books illustrated with photographs, and it laid the foundations of the modern study of emotion. It is also one of Darwin's most charming books, full of dogs, cats, monkeys and babies. It follows naturally from [The Descent of Man](/book/146?lang=en).

about: Opticks, published in 1704 and written in English rather than Latin, describes Isaac Newton's experiments with light: passing sunlight through prisms to show that white light is a mixture of colours, measuring how each colour bends, explaining the rainbow and the coloured rings that appear between two pieces of glass. The book ends with a series of open questions about light, matter and gravity.
context: Newton delayed the book until after the death of his rival Robert Hooke. Its method of patient experiment made it a model for science, and it continued a tradition that goes back to the Arab scholar [Ibn al-Haytham](/author/haytham?lang=en), whose Book of Optics had transformed the study of light seven centuries earlier.

about: Written by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels for a small group of German workers in London and published in February 1848, the Manifesto opens with 'A spectre is haunting Europe' and closes with 'Workers of all countries, unite!' In between it tells history as a series of class struggles and describes, with surprising admiration, how the bourgeoisie had transformed the world.
context: It is short enough to read in an afternoon, and whatever one thinks of the movements and states that later claimed it, few pamphlets have had such influence. Its pages on globalisation and constant economic change can sound remarkably current; read it beside John Stuart Mill's [Principles of Political Economy](/book/267?lang=en) for the other side of the debate.

about: In 1795, as the wars of revolutionary France raged, the philosopher Immanuel Kant wrote a short essay in the form of a peace treaty. Its preliminary articles forbid secret clauses, standing armies and interference in other states; its definitive articles call for republican government, a federation of free states and a right of hospitality for every stranger on earth.
context: Kant's title came, he said, from a Dutch innkeeper's sign that showed a graveyard. The essay is often cited as an ancestor of the League of Nations and the United Nations, and it is the most accessible way into a philosopher better known for difficult books.

about: Freud's most important book, published at the turn of 1900, argues that dreams are not random but the disguised fulfilment of wishes, and that they can be interpreted. He distinguishes the remembered dream from its hidden thoughts and explains the work of condensation and displacement that turns one into the other, using many of his own dreams as examples, starting with the famous dream of Irma's injection.
context: Freud called the interpretation of dreams the royal road to the unconscious. The book sold only a few hundred copies at first but went on to shape psychology, literature and film. Modern science has questioned much of it; as the founding text of psychoanalysis, it remains essential.

about: In four essays published in 1913, Freud turned psychoanalysis toward anthropology. Starting from the taboos and totem animals described by travellers and anthropologists, he compares them with the obsessions of his patients and ends with a bold theory: that religion and morality began with a prehistoric crime, the killing of a tyrannical father by his sons.
context: Few anthropologists accept the theory today, and Freud built it on the sources of his time. But the book is a key to how he thought about guilt, law and religion, and it led to his later writings on civilisation. Read it after [A General Introduction to Psychoanalysis](/book/162?lang=en).

about: Published in 1905, these three essays set out Freud's theory of human development: that sexual drives are present from early childhood, that they pass through stages, and that adult character and neurosis are shaped by how those stages are lived. Freud discusses what was then called deviation calmly and clinically, and the book caused a scandal in the Vienna of its day.
context: This is the English translation by A. A. Brill, published under this title. Together with [The Interpretation of Dreams](/book/159?lang=en), it is one of the two pillars of psychoanalytic theory, and Freud kept revising it for twenty years. It is a work of medical science written for adult readers.

about: Freud gave these lectures at the University of Vienna between 1915 and 1917 to an audience of doctors and laypeople, and they remain the clearest introduction to his ideas in his own words. He begins with everyday slips of the tongue and forgotten names, moves to dreams, and ends with the theory of the neuroses.
context: The tone is that of a patient teacher who anticipates objections and answers them. If you want to understand what psychoanalysis claims before deciding what you think of it, start here, then go on to [The Interpretation of Dreams](/book/159?lang=en).

about: After the First World War Freud met a puzzle his theory could not explain: soldiers who relived their trauma in nightmares, and patients who repeated painful experiences instead of avoiding them. In this short book of 1920 he describes his grandson's game of throwing away a toy and pulling it back, and proposes a second basic drive alongside the drive for life and pleasure: a drive toward death.
context: The idea of the death drive was controversial even among Freud's followers, but it changed his whole theory and influenced philosophy and literature for decades. It is a speculative book, and Freud says so himself, which makes it one of his most adventurous.

about: In 1923 Freud introduced the model of the mind that most people know today: the id, the reservoir of drives; the ego, which deals with reality; and the superego, the inner voice of conscience formed from parents and society. He compares the ego to a rider trying to guide a horse that is much stronger than he is.
context: It is a short and fairly technical book, but these three terms entered everyday language, and the later works of psychoanalysis build on them. Read it after [Beyond the Pleasure Principle](/book/163?lang=en), which it continues.

about: Faust, a scholar who has studied everything and found no satisfaction, makes a wager with the devil Mephistopheles: if Mephistopheles can ever give him a moment so perfect that he wishes it to last, he may take his soul. What follows takes Faust from a student tavern and a witches' kitchen to the tragic love story of Gretchen, a young woman whose life he destroys.
context: Goethe worked on Faust for almost sixty years; Part One appeared in 1808 and Part Two after his death in 1832. It is the central work of German literature, here in an English verse translation. Read [The Sorrows of Young Werther](/book/166?lang=en) to see the young Goethe first.

about: Werther, a sensitive young man, spends a summer in a country town and falls hopelessly in love with Lotte, who is engaged to the sensible, decent Albert. His letters to a friend tell of happiness in nature, children and poetry, then of jealousy, humiliation and despair, until he borrows Albert's pistols.
context: Published in 1774, when Goethe was twenty-four, the novel made him famous across Europe overnight. Young men dressed like Werther in blue coats and yellow waistcoats, and Napoleon said he had read it seven times. It is short, intense and still the classic portrait of a love that consumes a whole life.

about: Wilhelm, the son of a prosperous merchant, dreams of the theatre and leaves home to join a troupe of travelling actors. Through love affairs, failed productions, a staging of Hamlet and the mysterious figures of the girl Mignon and the old Harper, he slowly learns that the life he imagined is not the one he is meant to lead.
context: Published in 1795 and 1796, this is the novel that defined the Bildungsroman, the story of a young person's education by life, a form later used by Dickens, Joyce and many others; Thomas Carlyle's translation brought it to English readers. Mignon's song 'Do you know the land where the lemon trees bloom?' became one of the most set poems in German music.

about: In the spring of 1300, halfway through his life, Dante finds himself lost in a dark wood. The Roman poet Virgil appears and leads him down through the nine circles of Hell, where he meets the lovers Paolo and Francesca and the starving Count Ugolino, then up the mountain of Purgatory, until Beatrice, the woman he loved in his youth, guides him through the spheres of Paradise to the vision of God.
context: Written in a hundred cantos of interlocking three-line stanzas, the Comedy shaped how Europe imagined the afterlife and turned Italian into a literary language. Scholars have long debated whether Dante knew the Latin translation of the story of the Prophet's Night Journey; readers of Arabic can compare it with al-Ma'arri's [Epistle of Forgiveness](/book/1965893?lang=en), another visit to the afterlife among poets.

about: Dante first saw Beatrice when they were both nine years old, and he spent the rest of his life writing about her. The New Life, finished around 1295, tells that story in short prose chapters that frame his own early poems: her greeting in the street, the pain of being ignored, the screen ladies he pretended to love, his dreams and her early death in 1290.
context: The book ends with a promise to write of Beatrice what had never been written of any woman, a promise kept in [The Divine Comedy](/book/170?lang=en). It is short, strange and tender, one of the first books in which a poet explains his own poems, and a key to the whole of Dante.

about: A retired professor arrives at his late first wife's country estate with his beautiful young second wife, and the household falls apart. Uncle Vanya, who has spent twenty-five years running the estate and sending its income to the professor, realises that the man he served is a fraud. The country doctor Astrov, who plants forests and drinks too much, falls for the young wife, while plain, devoted Sonya loves him in silence.
context: First staged by the Moscow Art Theatre in 1899, Uncle Vanya is a comedy of wasted lives in which almost nothing happens and everything changes. Sonya's final speech about the rest that awaits them is one of the most moving endings in theatre. Read it with [The Lady with the Dog](/book/178?lang=en) for Chekhov at his best.

about: Dmitri Gurov, a married Moscow banker who thinks of women as an amusing pastime, notices a young woman walking a small white dog along the seafront at Yalta. Their holiday affair is supposed to end when the season does, but back in Moscow he cannot forget Anna Sergeyevna, and he travels to her provincial town to find her at the theatre.
context: Published in 1899, this short story contains no great events and no clear ending, and it is often called one of the most perfect short stories ever written. In a few pages Chekhov shows how a careless man is changed, against his will, by real love, and leaves his lovers just as the hardest part begins.

about: Bedford, a bankrupt businessman hiding in the English countryside to write a play, meets Mr Cavor, an absent-minded scientist who has invented a substance that blocks gravity. Together they build a glass sphere and fly to the Moon, where they find a frozen world that comes alive with the lunar dawn and a vast civilisation of insect-like Selenites living in caverns beneath the surface.
context: Published in 1901, the novel is both a thrilling adventure and a satire of human greed, since Bedford sees the Moon mainly as a source of gold. Its picture of a society in which each creature is shaped for a single job is still unsettling. It belongs with [The Time Machine](/book/179?lang=en) among Wells's best scientific romances.

about: In about three hundred pages, H. G. Wells tells the whole story of the world, from the formation of the Earth and the first living things through the empires of the ancient world, the rise of Christianity and Islam, the Mongol conquests and the age of science, to the end of the First World War.
context: Published in 1922 as a shorter version of his bestselling Outline of History, it was written for ordinary readers who wanted the big picture, and it ends with the hope that humanity might unite before it destroyed itself. Some judgements now look dated, but the clarity and the sense of urgency remain impressive.

about: In 1751, after his father's death, seventeen-year-old David Balfour walks to the house of his uncle Ebenezer to claim his inheritance. The miserly uncle tries to kill him on a broken staircase, then has him kidnapped onto a ship bound for slavery in the Carolinas. On board David meets Alan Breck Stewart, a proud, vain and brave Highlander loyal to the defeated Jacobites, and the two end up fleeing across the Scottish Highlands, suspected of a real political murder.
context: Published in 1886, the same year as Jekyll and Hyde, Kidnapped is a perfect adventure novel and a moving story of friendship between two very different men. Readers who enjoyed [Treasure Island](/book/185?lang=en) will find Stevenson here at the height of his powers.

about: These sixty-odd poems look at the world from the height of a child: the shadow that grows and shrinks, the sheets of a sickbed turned into a land of hills and armies, the unfairness of going to bed in summer while it is still light, the lamplighter passing in the street at dusk.
context: Robert Louis Stevenson was often ill as a boy, and the book, published in 1885, is dedicated to his nurse, Alison Cunningham, who sat with him through long nights. The poems are simple enough to read aloud to small children and wise enough for their parents. For Stevenson's adventures, go on to [Treasure Island](/book/185?lang=en).

about: Six months after her trip to Wonderland, Alice climbs through the mirror above her fireplace into a world where everything runs backwards and the countryside is laid out like a chessboard. To become a queen she must cross it square by square, meeting Tweedledum and Tweedledee, Humpty Dumpty, the gentle White Knight and the Red Queen, who has to run as fast as she can just to stay in the same place.
context: Published in 1871, the sequel to [Alice's Adventures in Wonderland](/book/189?lang=en) is more mathematical and a little melancholy, and it gave English the nonsense poem 'Jabberwocky' and 'The Walrus and the Carpenter'. Carroll's logic jokes are as clever for adults as the adventures are for children.

about: A ship's crew sets out to hunt the Snark, a creature no one has ever described clearly, led by a Bellman whose map of the ocean is perfectly blank. The crew all have names beginning with B: a Baker who has forgotten his own name, a Butcher who can only kill beavers, a Banker, a Barrister and a Beaver who makes lace. The danger, they are warned, is that the Snark might turn out to be a Boojum.
context: Published in 1876 as 'an agony in eight fits', this is Lewis Carroll's longest nonsense poem, and people have argued about its meaning ever since, which is exactly the joke. It is great fun read aloud. For more of Carroll's nonsense verse, see [Through the Looking-Glass](/book/190?lang=en).

about: The little mermaid who gives up her voice for a pair of legs, the ugly duckling mocked by the farmyard, the little match girl on a freezing New Year's Eve, the emperor whose new clothes do not exist, the steadfast tin soldier and the snow queen with her splinter of ice: this collection gathers the tales that made Hans Christian Andersen the most loved storyteller of the nineteenth century.
context: Andersen, a poor shoemaker's son from Odense in Denmark, wrote more than a hundred and fifty tales, and unlike the folk stories collected by the [Brothers Grimm](/book/317?lang=en), most were his own inventions. Many end sadly, and they are as much about loneliness and longing as about magic.

about: In 1271 a seventeen-year-old Venetian named Marco Polo set out with his father and uncle for the court of Kublai Khan, and did not come home for twenty-four years. His book describes the Silk Road, the palaces of the Mongol emperor, the paper money, the coal that burned like wood, the postal relays and the great city of Hangzhou, as well as India, Persia and the lands of the Indian Ocean.
context: Marco dictated the book in a Genoese prison in 1298 to a writer of romances named Rustichello, which partly explains its mix of exact detail and wonder. Christopher Columbus carried an annotated copy. Medieval Arab travellers wrote about many of the same places: compare the journey of [Ibn Jubayr](/author/jubayr?lang=en).

about: Marcus Aurelius was the most powerful man in the world, emperor of Rome from 161 to 180, and he spent many of his last years on campaign along the Danube. At night in his tent he wrote notes to himself in Greek, never meant for publication: reminders to be patient with difficult people, to remember how short life is, to do his duty without complaining and to accept what he could not change.
context: The Meditations are the most personal document of Stoic philosophy and one of the most widely read books of antiquity today, beloved by soldiers, athletes and people going through hard times. Read a few entries a day rather than straight through; they were written that way.

about: The Analects are a collection of short sayings and conversations of Confucius, the teacher who lived in China between 551 and 479 BC, gathered by his disciples after his death. In brief exchanges he talks about how to become a good person, how to govern, how to honour one's parents and how to learn, returning again and again to humaneness, sincerity and proper conduct.
context: For two thousand years this small book shaped education, government and family life across East Asia. Many sayings are only a line or two long, so it rewards slow reading; set it beside [The Art of War](/book/256?lang=en) and the sayings of Lao Tzu for the other great voices of ancient Chinese thought.

about: Seventeen years before The Wealth of Nations, Adam Smith published a book on morality, and he valued it at least as highly. He argues that our moral sense grows from sympathy, our ability to imagine ourselves in another person's place, and from an imagined impartial spectator inside us who judges our conduct as an outsider would.
context: First published in 1759 and revised until Smith's death in 1790, the book shows that the father of modern economics was above all a moral philosopher who did not believe people act only out of self-interest. It owes much to his friend David Hume, whose [Treatise of Human Nature](/book/278?lang=en) it answers in places.

about: John Stuart Mill's essay of 1859 asks how far society may control the individual, and answers with a single principle: the only legitimate reason to use power over anyone against their will is to prevent harm to others. He defends freedom of thought and discussion, warns against the quiet tyranny of public opinion, and argues that individuality is necessary for human progress.
context: Mill dedicated the book to his wife, Harriet Taylor Mill, who had died the year before and with whom he had developed its ideas. It remains one of the most cited works in debates about free speech. Continue with [The Subjection of Women](/book/266?lang=en).

about: Mill's short book sets out and defends the principle that actions are right in so far as they tend to promote happiness. Against critics who called this a philosophy fit for pigs, he argues that some pleasures are higher than others, and writes the famous line that it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied, better Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.
context: First published as magazine essays in 1861, Utilitarianism is the clearest classic statement of a theory that still shapes economics, law and ethics, and its last chapter on justice is especially thoughtful. Read it with [On Liberty](/book/264?lang=en).

about: Published in 1869, this essay argues that the legal subordination of women to men, in marriage, property, education and the vote, is wrong in itself and a major obstacle to human progress. Mill dismantles the claim that women's nature makes them unsuited to public life, pointing out that no one can know women's nature while they are denied freedom.
context: Mill had already proposed votes for women in Parliament in 1867, and he credited his late wife Harriet Taylor and her daughter Helen with many of the ideas. It is a landmark of the movement for equal rights, building on [A Vindication of the Rights of Woman](/book/299?lang=en).

about: For half a century after its publication in 1848, this was the standard textbook of economics in the English-speaking world.
